summary: Specifies the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP), a message-oriented transport protocol that offers reliable delivery with features such as multiple streams and multihoming. It obsoletes RFC 4960 and folds in the chunk flags registry from RFC 6096 and the I bit of DATA chunks from RFC 7053. It also obsoletes the errata documents RFC 4460 and RFC 8540. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: SCTP is a transport protocol like TCP, but it keeps several independent streams of messages open at once, so a stalled message does not hold up the others. It also starts with a four-step handshake that protects the server against flood attacks, and it can use more than one network path.

what is a state cookie in sctp
subtitle: A transport protocol that keeps messages in separate ordered streams and can use several network paths at once.

tldr.problem: TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so a lost message holds up everything behind it, and its single-path design makes it awkward for a server with several network addresses. TCP is also relatively vulnerable to SYN-style denial-of-service attacks.
tldr.mechanism: SCTP adds an association with several streams, giving each message its own place in the order. It numbers every fragment separately for reliability, uses a four-way handshake with a cookie so the server commits no state until the client proves it can receive, and can send over several addresses.
tldr.outcome: One lost message no longer delays the others, and a failure of one path does not end the connection. This document obsoletes RFC 4960 and is a Proposed Standard from June 2022.

today: RFC 9260 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022. It obsoletes RFC 4960, and it also obsoletes RFC 6096, RFC 7053 and the errata documents RFC 4460 and RFC 8540. It has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: Why a Second Transport Protocol
sections.content:
TCP has performed immense service as the primary means of reliable data transfer in IP networks. However, an increasing number of recent applications have found TCP too limiting and have incorporated their own reliable data transfer protocol on top of UDP. The limitations users wished to bypass include the following.

TCP provides both reliable data transfer and strict order-of-transmission delivery of data. Some applications need reliable transfer without sequence maintenance, while others would be satisfied with partial ordering; in both cases the head-of-line blocking offered by TCP causes unnecessary delay. The stream-oriented nature of TCP is often an inconvenience, because applications add their own record marking to delineate their messages and make explicit use of the push facility to ensure that a complete message is transferred in a reasonable time. The limited scope of TCP sockets complicates the task of providing highly available data transfer capability using multi-homed hosts. And TCP is relatively vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks, such as SYN attacks.

Transport of PSTN signaling across the IP network is an application for which all of these limitations of TCP are relevant. While this application directly motivated the development of SCTP, other applications might find SCTP a good match to their requirements; one example is the use of data channels in the WebRTC infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP is a single pipe of bytes. If one piece is late, everything after it waits. SCTP was written for telephone signalling, where many small messages matter more than one smooth stream of bytes, and it is now also used for WebRTC data channels.

sections.title: Associations Instead of Connections
sections.content:
SCTP is viewed as a layer between the SCTP user application and a connectionless packet network service such as IP. The basic service offered by SCTP is the reliable transfer of user messages between peer SCTP users, and it performs this service within the context of an association between two SCTP endpoints.

SCTP is connection oriented in nature, but the association is a broader concept than the TCP connection. SCTP provides the means for each endpoint, during association startup, to give the other endpoint a list of transport addresses, that is multiple IP addresses in combination with an SCTP port, through which it can be reached and from which it will originate SCTP packets. The association spans transfers over all of the possible source and destination combinations that can be generated from each endpoint's lists.

In addition to encapsulating SCTP packets in IPv4 or IPv6, it is also possible to encapsulate SCTP packets in UDP or in DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side of an SCTP connection lists all the addresses it can be reached on. The connection then covers every combination of those addresses, so a failure of one path does not end it.

sections.title: Streams, Sequence Numbers and Bundling
sections.content:
A stream in SCTP refers to a sequence of user messages delivered in order with respect to other messages in the same stream, in contrast to TCP where the term refers to a sequence of bytes. At association startup the SCTP user can specify the number of streams to be supported, which is negotiated with the remote end. SCTP assigns a Stream Sequence Number to each message, and on the receiving side it ensures that messages are delivered in sequence within a given stream. While one stream might be blocked waiting for the next in-sequence message, delivery from other streams might proceed. A mechanism also exists for bypassing the sequenced delivery service, so that messages sent with it are delivered as soon as they are received.

When needed, SCTP fragments user messages so that the packet handed to the lower layer does not exceed the path MTU. Once a message has been fragmented, the fragmentation cannot be changed, and on receipt the fragments are reassembled into complete messages before being passed up.

SCTP assigns a Transmission Sequence Number (TSN) to each user data fragment or unfragmented message. The TSN is independent of any Stream Sequence Number assigned at the stream level. The receiving end acknowledges all TSNs received, even if there are gaps in the sequence, and a fragment that must be retransmitted keeps the TSN it was given. Reliable delivery is thus kept functionally separate from sequenced stream delivery.

An SCTP packet as delivered to the lower layer consists of a common header followed by one or more chunks. Bundling means carrying more than one chunk in the same packet. INIT, INIT ACK and SHUTDOWN COMPLETE chunks MUST NOT be bundled with any other chunk; all other chunks MAY be bundled into a packet that does not exceed the path MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are numbered twice. The stream number says where a message belongs in the order the application sees; the transmission number says where it sits in the stream of reliable delivery. That split is what lets one message be late without holding up the rest.

sections.title: Packets and Chunks
sections.content:
An SCTP packet is composed of a common header and chunks, and a chunk contains either control information or user data. All integer fields MUST be transmitted in network byte order.

The common header holds the source port number and the destination port number, both 16 bits, neither of which may be zero; a 32-bit Verification Tag; and a 32-bit checksum computed with the CRC32c algorithm. On transmit the Verification Tag MUST be set to the Initiate Tag received from the peer during association initialization, with three exceptions: a packet containing an INIT chunk MUST have a zero Verification Tag, a packet containing a SHUTDOWN COMPLETE chunk with the T bit set MUST copy the tag from the packet carrying the SHUTDOWN ACK chunk, and a packet containing an ABORT chunk MAY copy the tag from the packet that caused the abort. Packets received without the expected Verification Tag are discarded, which protects against blind masquerade attacks and against stale packets from a previous association. A packet with an invalid CRC32c checksum is silently discarded.

Each chunk has a Chunk Type, a Chunk Flags field, a Chunk Length and a Chunk Value. The chunk type takes a value from 0 to 254, with 255 reserved for future use as an extension field. The highest-order two bits of the chunk type say what to do with an unrecognized chunk: stop and discard the rest of the packet, stop and report it in an ERROR chunk, skip it and continue, or skip it and report it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet starts with two port numbers, a tag that proves the packet belongs to this connection, and a checksum. After that comes a list of chunks, each with a type number, so an unknown chunk can be skipped instead of breaking the connection.

sections.title: The Association States
sections.content:
During the lifetime of an association the endpoint moves between states in response to events. The events include SCTP user primitive calls such as ASSOCIATE, SHUTDOWN or ABORT, the reception of INIT, COOKIE ECHO, ABORT, SHUTDOWN and other control chunks, and timeout events.

The state diagram shows a path from CLOSED through COOKIE-WAIT and COOKIE-ECHOED to ESTABLISHED, then on to the shutdown states. From CLOSED, an ASSOCIATE creates the transport control block, sends an INIT and starts the T1-init timer, entering COOKIE-WAIT. On receiving a valid COOKIE ECHO the receiver creates the control block and sends a COOKIE ACK. The sender of the INIT enters COOKIE-ECHOED on receiving the INIT ACK, sends a COOKIE ECHO and starts the T1-cookie timer, and reaches ESTABLISHED on receiving the COOKIE ACK.

From ESTABLISHED the SHUTDOWN primitive checks outstanding DATA chunks and moves to SHUTDOWN-PENDING, and from there, when no more DATA chunks are outstanding, sends the SHUTDOWN chunk, starts the T2-shutdown timer and enters SHUTDOWN-SENT. On receiving a SHUTDOWN the peer enters SHUTDOWN-RECEIVED, and when its own data is done it sends a SHUTDOWN ACK and enters SHUTDOWN-ACK-SENT. Both paths end by sending SHUTDOWN COMPLETE and deleting the control block, returning to CLOSED. From any state, receiving an ABORT deletes the control block and sends an ABORT.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection has a small set of states. It starts closed, passes through two setup states, becomes established, and later goes through shutdown states before closing again. An abort can cut it short from anywhere.

sections.title: Starting an Association
sections.content:
An association is initiated by a request from the SCTP user. A cookie mechanism, similar to one described by Karn and Simpson, is employed during the initialization to provide protection against synchronization attacks. The cookie mechanism uses a four-way handshake, the last two legs of which are allowed to carry user data for fast setup.

In the normal case, A sends an INIT with its Initiate Tag and starts the T1-init timer, entering COOKIE-WAIT. Z composes a State Cookie and replies with an INIT ACK carrying the Verification Tag, its own Initiate Tag and the cookie. A cancels the T1-init timer, sends a COOKIE ECHO carrying the cookie, starts the T1-cookie timer and enters COOKIE-ECHOED. Z builds its control block, enters ESTABLISHED and replies with a COOKIE ACK. A cancels the T1-cookie timer and enters ESTABLISHED, and the two sides may then exchange data.

The cookie is what protects Z. Until the cookie comes back, Z has kept no state beyond the cookie itself, so a flood of INIT chunks costs the attacker, not the server. If the State Cookie in a received COOKIE ECHO chunk is invalid, the receiver MUST silently discard the packet; if it is expired, the receiver MUST send back an ERROR chunk. If the T1-init timer expires, the endpoint retransmits the INIT or COOKIE ECHO chunk with the same Initiate Tag or State Cookie and restarts the timer, and this is repeated Max.Init.Retransmits times before the endpoint considers the peer unreachable and reports the failure to its upper layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up takes four messages. The server sends back a signed ticket, the cookie, and only builds the connection when that ticket comes back. A flood of connection attempts therefore never makes the server reserve anything.

sections.title: Paths, Failures and Heartbeats
sections.content:
When the peer endpoint is multi-homed, an endpoint SHOULD keep an error counter for each of the peer's destination transport addresses. Each time the T3-rtx timer expires on any address, or a HEARTBEAT chunk sent to an idle address is not acknowledged within an RTO, the error counter of that address is incremented. When the counter exceeds the protocol parameter Path.Max.Retrans of that address, the endpoint SHOULD mark the address as inactive and notify the upper layer. When an outstanding TSN is acknowledged, or a heartbeat is answered, the counter SHOULD be cleared and the upper layer told that the address is active again.

When the primary path is marked inactive, the sender MAY automatically transmit new packets to an alternate destination address if one exists and is active; if more than one alternate is active, only one SHOULD be chosen.

By default an endpoint SHOULD monitor the reachability of idle destination addresses by sending HEARTBEAT chunks periodically. A destination transport address is considered idle if no new chunk that can be used for updating path round-trip time, and no HEARTBEAT chunk, has been sent to it within the current heartbeat period of that address. This applies to both active and inactive addresses.

Verification tags also protect against packets that arrive out of the blue. Packets whose Verification Tag does not match the one expected for the association are discarded, which stops an attacker from injecting packets into an established flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address of the peer has its own error counter. If retransmissions or unanswered heartbeats pile up on one address, that address is marked unusable and traffic moves to another one, while the connection stays up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As a common transport protocol designed to reliably carry time-sensitive user messages, such as billing or signalling messages for telephony services, SCTP has two security objectives: availability of reliable and timely data transport services, and integrity of the user-to-user information carried by SCTP.

For data corruption, where the risk of undetected errors is considered too great, additional integrity protection is required. The SCTP Authentication extension MAY be used when the threat environment requires stronger integrity protection but does not require confidentiality. For confidentiality, the risk usually applies to the signalling data payload rather than to the protocol overheads, so encryption of the user data alone might be considered, performed by the user application. Where the requirement includes masking of IP addresses and ports, as for mobile users, ESP SHOULD be used instead, with a cryptographic transform that includes integrity protection, and IKEv2 SHOULD be used for key management of ESP.

Blind denial-of-service attacks, where the attacker cannot see the traffic, take the form of flooding, masquerade or improper monopolization of services. Protection against flooding begins at the equipment design level, with measures such as avoiding commitment of limited resources before determining that the request is legitimate, giving priority to work in progress, removing duplicate or stale queued requests, and not responding to unexpected packets sent to non-unicast addresses. The design of SCTP is resistant to flooding attacks, particularly in its use of a four-way startup handshake, its use of a cookie to defer commitment of resources at the responding node until the handshake is completed, and its use of a Verification Tag to prevent insertion of extraneous packets into the flow of an established association.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP aims to stay available and to deliver the right bytes. It does not encrypt anything by itself: the RFC points at an authentication extension for stronger integrity, and at ESP for confidentiality, and it explains why the cookie and the tag make floods and injected packets hard to pull off.

messages.label: INIT
messages.note: Carries the Initiate Tag and the list of addresses.

messages.label: INIT ACK
messages.note: Carries the State Cookie; no server state is committed yet.

messages.label: COOKIE ECHO
messages.note: Returns the cookie, proving the client can receive.

fields.name: Source Port Number
fields.desc: The SCTP sender's port number; zero must not be used.

fields.name: Destination Port Number
fields.desc: The port the packet is destined for; zero must not be used.

fields.name: Verification Tag
fields.desc: The Initiate Tag received from the peer; a mismatch causes the packet to be discarded.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: CRC32c over the packet; an invalid checksum means the packet is silently discarded.

fields.name: Chunk Type
fields.desc: Identifies the information in the chunk value; values 0 to 254 are used.

fields.name: Chunk Flags
fields.desc: Flags whose meaning depends on the chunk type.

fields.name: Chunk Length
fields.desc: Length of the chunk in bytes, including the header.

fields.name: Chunk Value
fields.desc: The information carried by the chunk.

items.label: INIT ACK
items.desc: Answers an INIT and carries the State Cookie.

items.label: SACK
items.desc: Cumulative acknowledgement of transmission sequence numbers.

items.label: HEARTBEAT
items.desc: Checks that a path is still working.

items.label: COOKIE ECHO
items.desc: Returns the State Cookie to the server.

items.label: COOKIE ACK
items.desc: Confirms that the cookie was accepted.
